PORTAL HYPERTENSION

Slide 2

Portal Hypertension

Slide 3
  • Hepatic Portal Flow :
    • around 1 L / minute
    • Indirectly regulated by vasoconstriction and vasodilatation of mesenteric arteries.
    • Drains most of the gastrointestinal system.
  • Definition :
    • Normal Portal pressure is around 5-10 mmHg
    • PHTN defined as PP > 12 mmHg ( 25 cm H2O)
Notes

Topic 1 · Portal Hypertension

Portal Circulation — Basics

CORE NUMBERS
Hepatic portal blood flow ≈ 1 L/min; drains blood from most of the GI tract into the liver.
Portal veins have little/no muscular control — portal flow is modified mainly indirectly, via changes in arterial inflow.
Normal portal pressure ≈ 5–10 mmHg. IVC/right atrial pressure ≈ 0 mmHg (may go negative on inspiration) — this gradient drives portal venous return.
DEFINITION
Portal hypertension = persistent portal pressure >12 mmHg (this lecture). Must be persistent — coughing, sneezing, and ↑intra-abdominal pressure only transiently raise portal pressure.
Slide 4

Pathophysiology

Slide 5
  • Pressure ( P ) = Flow ( F ) x Resistance ( R)
    • Change in R is the primary and initial factor for increasing P.
    • In most cases, F increases as consequence, contributing and aggravating PHTN.
  • Causes :
    • PreHepatic.
    • Hepatic.
    • PostHepatic.
Notes

Pathophysiology

Initial abnormality is usually ↑vascular resistance to portal flow. The compensatory ↑portal/splanchnic blood flow that tries to overcome this resistance further raises portal pressure. Concept: pressure gradient = flow × resistance.

Causes

Slide 6
  • PreHepatic :
    • Most common cause is portal vein thrombosis.
      • PVT is the most common cause of PHTN in children.
    • Congenital Atresia, extrinsic compression, splenic vein thrombosis.
  • Hepatic : can be divided in three types :
    • Pre-Sinusoidal : Schistosomiasis, Granulomatous disease.
    • Sinusoidal : cirrhosis, amyloidosis, congenital fibrosis.
  • PostHepatic :
    • Hepatic venous occlusion.
    • Constrictive pericarditis, Heart failure.
Notes

Portal Venous Anatomy

SMV + splenic vein → portal vein
Portal vein → right + left portal branches
IMV may drain into the splenic vein, the SMV, or near the splenoportal confluence
IMV can generally be ligated without major consequence
Acute major SMV obstruction → severe intestinal ischemia
Chronic SMV obstruction may be tolerated as collaterals develop
Notes

Causes of Portal Hypertension — by Site of Obstruction

Classification of Portal Hypertension

SiteCauseKey Notes
Pre-hepaticPortal vein thrombosis (PVT)Most common pre-hepatic cause; important cause in children
Extrinsic compression of the portal venous system—
Splenic vein thrombosisLeft-sided portal hypertension, predominantly left-sided collaterals
HepaticPre-sinusoidalResistance before blood enters sinusoids/hepatocytes
SinusoidalResistance within liver parenchyma/sinusoids — cirrhosis = major cause
Post-sinusoidalObstruction after sinusoidal passage
Post-hepaticHepatic vein occlusion (Budd–Chiari syndrome)—
Heart failure↑venous/right-sided pressure → back-pressure into hepatic/portal circulation
  • Post-hepatic cause of portal hypertension → Budd–Chiari syndrome. 429
  • Variceal bleeding with splenomegaly, normal portal vein and liver → left-sided (sinistral) portal hypertension (splenic vein thrombosis) 439; recurrent pancreatitis, isolated fundal varices, thrombosed splenic vein → splenectomy. 435 ×8

Cirrhosis

Slide 7
  • The final stage of chronic liver diseases leading to irreversible diffuse fibrosis of the liver with formation of regenerative nodules.
  • Major predisposing condition to HCC
  • Complications :
    • Juandice .
    • PHTN : most common eitology.
    • Coagulation defects.
    • Ascites.
    • Hepatic encephalopathy.
    • Hyperestrinisim : Gynecomastia and spider telangiectasia.
Notes

Cirrhosis

DEFINITION
Cirrhosis = final stage of chronic liver disease, with irreversible diffuse fibrosis and liver damage. It is the most common cause of portal hypertension and a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
Notes

Major Complications

Jaundice
Portal hypertension
Coagulopathy
Ascites
Hepatic encephalopathy
Hyperestrogenism
MECHANISM — HYPERESTROGENISM
Reduced hepatic metabolism of estrogen → gynecomastia, loss of body hair, and spider angiomas.
  • Element of the Child-Pugh score → serum albumin (with total bilirubin, INR, ascites, encephalopathy). 436 ×2
Slide 8Cirrhosis
  • Assessment of the underlaying eitology
    • Hx and Ex
    • blood work : basic, haematological and viral test
    • Imaging : US, CT, MRI +\- Fibro scan
    • Endoscopic : assessing and managing varices.
  • management and surveillance.
Notes

Assessment of Cirrhosis

ModalityRole
History & ExaminationBaseline clinical assessment
LaboratoryBasic bloods + viral hepatitis testing
Imaging (US/CT/MRI)Assessment and HCC surveillance
FibroScanAssesses liver stiffness/elasticity; fibrosis staged, early stages may be reversible
EXAM TRAP
FibroScan is used mainly in pre-cirrhotic fibrosis — it is not used to diagnose already-established cirrhosis in this lecture.
RULE OF THUMB — CIRRHOSIS SURVEILLANCE
All cirrhotic patients need regular surveillance for two life-threatening complications: ultrasound (HCC) and upper GI endoscopy (esophageal/gastric varices).

Complications of PHTN

Slide 9
  • Ascites : exacerbation and maintenance
  • Porto-systemic collaterals :
    • Gastro-Esophageal : LGV with esophageal veins
    • Umbilical
    • Ano-rectal : SRV with M&IRV
    • Veins of Retzius
Notes

Complications of Portal Hypertension

Ascites

↑Portal hydrostatic pressure → fluid movement into the peritoneal cavity. Severe/refractory ascites can impair walking, breathing, and eating.
WARNING
Repeated paracentesis carries infection risk; infected ascites may become loculated/septated, making later drainage more difficult.
Notes

Portosystemic Collaterals

Portal blood seeks a lower-resistance route back to systemic circulation → formation/enlargement of collaterals.

Major Portosystemic Collateral Sites

SiteDescription
Gastroesophageal varicesMost clinically significant — see below
Umbilical varicesRecanalized paraumbilical veins → caput medusae
Anorectal varicesSuperior rectal ↔ inferior rectal vein communication
Veins of RetziusSmall retroperitoneal portosystemic collateral veins
Umbilical Varices — Caput MedusaeRecanalized/enlarged paraumbilical veins radiate from the umbilicus. May coexist with gynecomastia, loss of body hair, and ascites. Local/pre-hepatic obstruction may cause abdominal collaterals without systemic cirrhosis stigmata.
DANGER — SURGICAL TRAP
A portal-hypertensive umbilical varix can be mistaken for an umbilical hernia (ascites itself also predisposes to true umbilical hernia). Operating on an unrecognized large umbilical varix can cause massive hemorrhage. Always examine the abdominal wall carefully, including standing.

Umbilical Hernia vs. Umbilical Varix

Umbilical HerniaUmbilical Varix / Caput Medusae
NatureReducible bulge through an abdominal wall defectPersistent dilated venous swelling (portal hypertension)
On lying downMay reduce/changePersists (engorged veins)
Anorectal VaricesArise from communication between the superior rectal vein and the inferior rectal vein (which drains to the IVC). Must be distinguished from hemorrhoids to avoid severe bleeding from inappropriate intervention.
FindingAppearance
Anorectal varicesTortuous, longitudinal, snake-like veins
HemorrhoidsTear-shape / droplet-like protrusions
Esophageal Varices requires endoscopic surveillance.Dilated submucosal veins, classically in the lower third of the esophagus, caused by portal hypertension. Every cirrhotic patient
HIGH-YIELD NUMBERS
Esophageal varices: seen in ≈80% of decompensated cirrhosis; gastric varices ≈10–15%
Variceal bleeding contributes to roughly 1/3 of cirrhosis deaths — hence regular endoscopic surveillance
≈40% of varices may bleed spontaneously
Acid reflux has been proposed as a precipitant of rupture, but this is not proven

Esophageal Varcies

Slide 16
  • Dilated submucosal veins, located in the lower third of the esophagus.
  • Every pt with suspicion or diagnosis of cirrhosis should undergo EGD for screening, absence doesn’t exclude PHTN.
  • Present in around 80% of decompensated cirrhosis, with 5-10 % have associated gastric varies.
  • Responsible for more than 30% of all deaths in pts with cirrhosis.

Acute Variceal Bleed

Slide 17
  • More than 40% bleed spontaneously, or it could be secondary to acid reflux.
  • Acute Variceal bleeding mortality rate ranges from 20%-50% depending on the hepatic reserve and severity of cirrhosis.
  • Hemorrhage is frequently massive, accompanied by hematemesis and hemodynamic instability.
  • Rebleed rates after episode of acute bleeding could reach upto 70% in non-treated patients.
  • Alcoholic with massive haematemesis, splenomegaly and ascites → oesophageal varices. 429
  • The IV drug shown to reduce mortality in variceal bleeding → ceftriaxone (antibiotics) 438 ×6; cirrhotic with massive haematemesis, hypotension and stigmata → IV antibiotics. 437 ×3
Notes

Acute Variceal Hemorrhage

CLINICAL FEATURES
Usually massive upper GI bleeding, frequently with hemodynamic instability/shock. Mortality ≈20–50%, strongly dependent on hepatic reserve. After one bleed, rebleeding risk is high (persistent portal hypertension).
Slide 18Acute Variceal Bleed
  • Start with your ABC.
  • Resuscitation with PRBCs and blood products.
  • Correct coagulation deficits.
  • Broad spectrum IV Abx
    • It reduces risk of infection by 50% and improves survival.
    • should be given for total of 7 days.
  • Pharmacotherapy: Splancnic vasoconstriction.
    • Vassoprrssin vs Telipressin
    • Somatostatin vs octeriotide
      • IV Bolus then Infusion x 5 days.
Order: ABC → resuscitation (PRBCs, blood products, correct coagulopathy) → broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (7 days) → splanchnic vasoconstrictor (octreotide/somatostatin or terlipressin, bolus then infusion × 5 days) → urgent endoscopy.
Notes

Stepwise Management

1 ABC first. Airway: massive hematemesis → major aspiration risk, may need intubation. Breathing: assess as in any unstable
patient. Circulation: rapid resuscitation, uncrossmatched blood products if severe, then tailor to coagulation studies.
2 Broad-spectrum antibiotics. Improve survival — variceal bleeding + cirrhosis carries septicemia risk up to ≈50%. Continue
≈7 days even if cultures are negative.
3 Reduce portal/splanchnic flow. Octreotide: bolus then continuous infusion for ≈5 days, to cause splanchnic
vasoconstriction.
4 Urgent endoscopy — diagnostic (confirms source — ≈30% of upper GI bleeds in cirrhotics are non-variceal) and
therapeutic.
  • After fluid resuscitation in a cirrhotic vomiting blood → octreotide. 437 ×7
  • Blood around the mouth after haematemesis in a cirrhotic → first immediate fluid resuscitation (ABC; endoscopy is definitive) 431 ×4; varices "all except" → immediate laparotomy is not part of management. 426
Slide 19Acute Variceal Bleed
  • Endoscopic Therapy :
    • Mainstay of management.
    • effective in controlling bleeding in around 90% of variceal bleed.
    • around 25-30 % are non-variceal origin.
    • two types of interventions :
      • Endoscopic sclerotherapy.
      • Endoscopic Band ligation.
  • Most effective treatment once bleeding varices are seen on endoscopy → endoscopic sclerotherapy (banding preferred today). 439 ×4
Slide 20

Endoscopic Therapy

Slide 21
  • Sclerotherapy:
    • Scelerosing agent injected in or around varix.
    • easier during bleeding, but with around 25% have complications
    • complications include : perforation, stricture, ulceration, systemic leak.
    • Higher rebelled rates, might require unto 3 treatments in 24hrs.
  • Band Ligation:
    • Less rates of complications
    • less rates of rebleed.

Acute Variceal Bleed

Slide 22
  • Balloon Tamponade:
    • around 10% of pts will not stop bleeding with previous interventions.
    • tube used to tamponade esophageal and gastric varices.
    • controls bleeding in 85% of cases.
    • Temporary control, for transfer or surgery.
    • high rate of rebleed after deflation ( ~ 50%)
    • high complication rates:
      • ischemia and necrosis
      • perforation
  • Oesophageal varices are treated by all except electrotherapy (keyed). 426
  • Bleeding not controlled by endoscopy, BP 80/40, HR 160 → Minnesota (balloon) tube as a bridge. 426
Notes

Endoscopic Techniques

Sclerotherapy vs. Band Ligation (EVL)

Endoscopic SclerotherapyBand Ligation (EVL)
TechniqueSclerosing agent injected into/around the varixBand placed over varix → mechanical occlusion
AdvantageUseful when active bleeding obscures the exact bleeding pointLower complication rate, lower rebleeding rate
DisadvantageHigher complications (perforation, stricture, ulceration, systemic); higher rebleedingHarder to place during extremely active massive bleeding
Preferred forSevere active bleeding with poor visualizationOngoing eradication / secondary prophylaxis
Balloon Tamponade
RULE OF THUMB
A last-resort, temporary bridge — NOT definitive treatment. Used when endoscopic control fails, endoscopy is unavailable, or to stabilize before definitive therapy. Initial control ≈85%, but rebleeding >50% after removal.

Tubes: Sengstaken–Blakemore (gastric aspiration lumen, gastric balloon, esophageal balloon) and Minnesota tube (adds an esophageal aspiration lumen). Requires endotracheal intubation; complications include esophageal/gastric ischemia, perforation, and aspiration.

CRITICAL SAFETY STEP
Never inflate the gastric balloon before confirming radiographically that it is below the diaphragm/in the stomach — incorrect inflation can cause catastrophic rupture/perforation.

Balloon Tamponade

Slide 23
  • Technically challenging.
  • all pts need to be intubated.
  • Sengstaken–Blakemore Vs Minnesota Tubes.

TIPS

Slide 24
  • Transjegular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt
    • Done percutaneously, to bypass the liver.
    • Only in PHTN of hepatic origin
    • Indications :
      • refractory acute bleeding (despite medical and endoscopic therapy)
      • recurrent life threatening variceal bleeds
      • refractory ascites in cirrhosis patients.
    • Done usually as bridging or palliative measure.
Notes

TIPS — Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt

Interventional radiology shunt between portal and systemic venous circulation, bypassing the high-resistance cirrhotic liver. Most useful for hepatic-origin portal hypertension; usually a bridge/palliative measure, not a cure.

IndicationDetail
Refractory acute variceal bleedingPersists despite resuscitation, drugs, and endoscopic treatment; especially with massive/repeated transfusion
Recurrent life-threatening bleedingDespite appropriate endoscopic management
Refractory/recurrent ascitesReduces portal pressure/ascites formation
COMPLICATIONS
Right heart failure — ↑venous return/preload from direct portal-to-systemic shunting
Hepatic encephalopathy — new or worsened, may progress to coma (bypassed hepatic detoxification)
Shunt stenosis/thrombosis
Worsening liver failure — blood diverted from an already diseased liver

Surgical portosystemic shunts (e.g. portocaval shunt) follow the same bypass concept but are rarely used now given TIPS; cirrhotic patients are poor operative candidates (coagulopathy, ascites, poor hepatic reserve). Older shunts may still appear in exams.

Slide 26TIPS
  • PTFE or metal stents
  • contra-indications:
    • RHF
    • severe encephalopathy
  • Complications:
    • hepatic encephalopathy (50%)
    • Stenosis & Thrombosis
    • worsening liver failure
  • Stable patient, contrast blush on CT angiography → angioembolisation. 439 ×2

Surgery For PHTN

Slide 27
  • Surgical shunts
    • non-selective
    • selective
      • Distal Splenorenal Shunts
    • Partial.
  • Devascularization procedures
Notes

Definitive Treatment

For portal hypertension from end-stage cirrhosis: liver transplantation. Note — transplant will not necessarily correct portal hypertension from extrahepatic disease (e.g. extensive PVT), depending on thrombosis location/extent.
Slide 28
Slide 29Surgery For PHTN
  • Liver Transplantation
    • not treatment for PHTN per se, but it is the best.
    • For liver related diseases.
      • Cirrhosis ( HBV, HCV, Alcoholic, PBC) - child B & C
      • Acute failure
      • Other ( Wilson, malignancies)
Slide 30

Variceal Prophylaxis

Slide 31
  • Primary Prophylaxis:
    • all pts with cirrhosis should have screening EGD.
    • 𝛽 - Blockers
      • reduces portal pressure by splanchnic vasoconstriction .
    • + \ - Endoscopic band ligation.
  • Secondary prophylaxis
    • After initial bleed
    • combined 𝛽 - Blockers + serial EBL
  • Newly diagnosed cirrhosis with visible varices — prevent the first bleed → propranolol. 437 ×4
Notes

Variceal Prophylaxis

Primary vs. Secondary Prophylaxis

SettingApproach
PrimaryCirrhosis/varices, never bled — all cirrhotics get screening endoscopyIf varices found → non-selective β-blocker
SecondaryAlready had a variceal bleed — requires continued surveillanceBand ligation + β-blocker (sclerotherapy not preferred here)

Notes

Mastery Checklist — Portal Hypertension

1 Portal HTN = persistent portal pressure >12 mmHg; SMV + splenic vein → portal vein.
2 PVT = most common pre-hepatic cause and the key cause in children; splenic vein thrombosis → left-sided portal HTN.
3 Cirrhosis = most common overall cause of portal hypertension; surveil with US (HCC) + endoscopy (varices).
4 Caput medusae can mimic umbilical hernia — unrecognized surgery risks catastrophic hemorrhage.
5 Anorectal varices (snake-like) vs. hemorrhoids (droplet-like) — must distinguish before intervening.
6 Acute variceal bleed order: ABC → antibiotics → octreotide → urgent endoscopy.
7 Band ligation > sclerotherapy for routine/secondary use (fewer complications, less rebleeding); sclerotherapy may help when
active bleeding obscures the view.
8 Balloon tamponade = temporary bridge only; confirm gastric balloon position below the diaphragm before inflating.
9 TIPS for refractory/recurrent variceal bleeding or refractory ascites; risks right heart failure & hepatic encephalopathy.
10 Definitive cure for end-stage cirrhotic portal HTN = liver transplant; prophylaxis = β-blocker (primary) or band ligation + β-
blocker (secondary).

Splenic Trauma

Slide 34
Notes

Topic 2 · Splenic Disorders

Splenic Anatomy & Trauma

ANATOMY
Spleen sits in the left upper quadrant, closely related to the stomach, pancreas, colon, and left kidney. Rich arterial/venous supply means trauma can cause major hemorrhage.
Slide 35Splenic Trauma
  • Can be managed by
    • Non-Operatively :
      • By interventional radiology
        • Selective or non-selective embolisation
      • low grade injury.
      • HD stability
      • no peritonitis and no other indications for laparotomy.
  • Splenic laceration 2 cm (1–3 cm parenchymal depth) → grade II. 441
  • Contraindication to non-operative management (keyed) → being in a peripheral hospital (no IR/ICU/24-h surgeon — operate or transfer). 437
Notes

Management of Splenic Trauma

CT may show a fractured spleen surrounded by blood; hemoperitoneum can also collect around the liver/other structures.

RULE OF THUMB
Non-operative management is preferred whenever appropriate: hemodynamically stable, low/medium-grade injury, no other injury requiring laparotomy.
OptionDetail
ObservationSmall injuries may stop bleeding spontaneously — monitor only
Selective embolizationPreferred. Interventional radiology embolizes the specific bleeding branch — preserves more viable spleen
Non-selective/proximal embolizationEmbolizes the main/proximal splenic artery; used when selective not feasible — greater risk of later splenic complications
WHEN SURGERY IS NEEDED
Hemodynamic instability or another injury requiring laparotomy (e.g. a major gastric laceration) — the spleen may then also require operative management.

Splenic preservation: in adults, splenectomy is the main operative procedure when removal is definitively required. In pediatric patients there is a strong effort to preserve/delay splenectomy (infectious risk); preservation/autotransplantation techniques exist but are beyond this lecture's scope.

  • Left-sided impact with left 7th–10th rib fractures → splenic laceration. 439
Slide 36Splenic Trauma
  • Operatively:
    • Splenectomy vs splenorraphy vs partial
      • laparotomy vs laparoscopy
    • Splenectomy in paediatrics
      • try to preserve the spleen as much as possible
  • Unstable, haemoperitoneum, laparotomy for a splenic haematoma → total splenectomy. 437 ×2
Slide 37

Splenic Artery Aneurysm

Slide 38
  • High risk for bleeding spontaneously
  • Treatment is indicated for :
    • Pseudo-aneurysms
      • symptomatic.
      • aneurysm size more 2 cm.
  • By IR vs surgery.
Notes

Splenic Artery Aneurysm, Cysts & Tumors

Splenic Artery Aneurysm

DANGER
Risk of spontaneous rupture/hemorrhage, particularly important in women of childbearing age/pregnancy. A pseudoaneurysm lacks a complete arterial wall → particularly high rupture risk.
INDICATIONS FOR TREATMENT
Pseudoaneurysm
Symptomatic aneurysm
Size >2 cm
Options: endovascular embolization, covered stent (selected cases), or surgery/splenectomy when required.
  • Symptomatic 5-cm splenic artery aneurysm, planning pregnancy → splenectomy; vaccinate 2–3 weeks pre-op. 437 ×2

Splenic Cysts

Slide 39
  • Divided into:
    • Pseudo-cysts:
      • not lined with epithelium
      • most common non-parasitic cyst.
      • commonly due to trauma
    • True non-infectious cysts:
      • Rare and usually asymptomatic.
      • Mostly present since birth.
      • Cancers could present as true cyst.
    • Both Treated only if symptomatic.
      • Resection vs splenectomy.

Splenic cysts

Slide 40
  • Parasitic cysts:
    • Most common true cysts.
    • common in endemic areas with parasitic diseases (e.g echinococcus spp).
    • Hydatid cysts presents as multiple daughter cysts or calcification in the wall.
    • Just like Liver Hydatid cysts, serological testing is important for Dx.
    • Intra-op , cyst injected with 3% Sodium Chloride to prevent spillage and subsequent anaphylactic shock.

Splenic Malignancies

Slide 41
  • Non-hematologic Tumors:
    • rare site for metastasis.
    • AngioSarcoma:
      • Aggressive with poor prognosis.
      • Linked to environmental exposures.
    • Hemangioma and lymphangioma
      • Benign conditions
    • Treatment === > Splenectomy
Notes

Splenic Cysts

TypeNotes
PseudocystMost common; related to previous trauma — heals leaving a cystic cavity with no true epithelial lining
True cystMuch rarer; usually benign
Parasitic cystManaged like parasitic hepatic cysts
Splenic TumorsVery large/extensive splenic cysts may require splenectomy.
• Hemangioma / lymphangioma — usually benign• Spleen is a rare site of solid-organ metastasis despite its rich blood supply
• Angiosarcoma — rare primary malignant tumor, very poor prognosis, splenectomy when treatable
• Non-Hodgkin lymphoma involves the spleen more often than Hodgkin lymphoma
  • The most commonly injured organ in blunt abdominal trauma → spleen. 442 ×2
Slide 42Splenic Malignancies
  • Hematologic Tumors :
    • Hodgkin’s Disease:
    • Non-Hodkin’s Lymphoma
      • NHL is more common in involving the spleen.
      • pt with symptoms related to Hypersplenism ( splenomegaly, Thrombocytopenia)
      • Splenectomy may be required:
        • Diagnosis
        • If pt us symptomatic
        • Disease mostly involving the spleen.
Notes

Hematological Disorders Involving the Spleen

Splenic involvement (e.g. lymphoma) can cause hypersplenism: splenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, bleeding/cytopenic symptoms.

Indications for Splenectomy in Hematological Disease

Diagnostic uncertainty requiring tissue diagnosis
Symptomatic splenomegaly/hypersplenism
Disease predominantly localized to the spleen
Selected CLL/CML cases after hematology referral
Slide 43Splenic Malignancies
  • Hematologic Tumors :
    • Hairy Cell Leukemia , CLL & CML:
      • Rare
      • Indications for splenectomy:
        • Infectious neutropenia
        • hemorrhage from thrombocytopenia

Splenic Disorders

Slide 44
  • Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura ( ITP):
    • Thrombocytopenia ( < 100,000) with normal bone marrow.
    • Antibody mediated platelets destruction.
    • Most common in women age 10-40 yrs.
    • Presents as :purpura, bruising, epistaxis and gingival bleeding.
    • Diagnosis of exclusion.
  • 38-year-old woman, gum bleeding, bruising, epistaxis, ITP (keyed) → splenectomy. 437 ×3
Slide 45Splenic Disorders
  • Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura ( ITP):
    • Treatment depends on severity.
      • Observation vs Steroids vs Plts transfusion vs IVIG
      • Splenectomy indicated in :
        • count < 10,000 for 6 wks or longer.
        • Thrombocytopenia refractory to steroids.
        • Thrombocytopenia with toxic side effects of steroids.
Notes

Immune Thrombocytopenia (ITP)

Immune-mediated platelet destruction → isolated thrombocytopenia with otherwise normal marrow production. More common in females, roughly 10–40 years. May present with petechiae/purpura, mucosal bleeding, genital bleeding. Diagnosis of exclusion. Initial management: observation, steroids, IVIG, or supportive transfusion depending on severity.

INDICATIONS FOR SPLENECTOMY
Platelets <10,000/µL persisting ≥6 weeks — major spontaneous bleeding risk
Steroid-refractory thrombocytopenia
Significant steroid toxicity making continued therapy unsuitable
Slide 46Splenic Disorders
  • Hereditary Spherocytosis:
    • AD disorder
    • RBCs deformed ( sphere shaped rather than biconcave)
    • Fragile, destroyed once they pass the splenic sinusoids.
    • Hemolysis causing:
      • Anemia, Juandice, splenomegaly and cholelithiasis.
      • Diagnosis: examination of a peripheral blood smear, increased reticulocyte count, increased osmotic fragility, and a negative Coombs’ test.
    • Treatment
      • Splenectomy after the age of 6 years.
      • It will correct the anemia, not the deformity.
Notes

Hereditary Spherocytosis

Autosomal dominant RBC membrane disorder. RBCs become spherical instead of biconcave; spherocytes retain oxygen-carrying capacity but are fragile and preferentially destroyed in the spleen → chronic hemolysis → anemia + jaundice. Diagnosis: spherocytes on peripheral blood film. Treatment: splenectomy.

KEY CONCEPT
Splenectomy does not correct the underlying genetic/RBC shape defect — spherocytes remain. It removes their major site of destruction, so hemolysis ↓ and anemia/symptoms improve. It treats the consequence, not the cause.

Splenectomy

Slide 47
  • Can be done open or laparoscopic.
  • Preparation for Surgery:
    • Elective Splenectomy should receive vaccination 2-3 week before surgery.
    • Emergency Splenectomy vacations given 2 weeks after
      • Or in case of trauma and fear of loss to follow up, can be given upon Discharge.
    • Vaccinations are for S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, and N. meningitides.
      • Re-vaccination is recommended for high risk individuals.
    • Abx prophylaxis post-op ?
  • Best way to reduce future infection before splenectomy → vaccinate against pneumococcus, meningococcus and H. influenzae b. 442 ×2
Notes

Splenectomy

Approach: open (generally for trauma) or laparoscopic (generally for elective conditions).

Notes

Vaccination Before/After Splenectomy

Vaccinate against major encapsulated organisms: pneumococcus, meningococcus, and Haemophilus influenzae type b.

SettingTiming
Elective splenectomy≈2–3 weeks before surgery, to allow protective antibody development
Emergency splenectomyVaccinate postoperatively; trauma patients ideally before discharge (follow-up may be unreliable)
Post-Splenectomy Complications
THROMBOCYTOSIS
Loss of splenic platelet sequestration/destruction → ↑platelet count → ↑thrombosis risk, particularly with underlying myeloproliferative disease.
OPSI — OVERWHELMING POST-SPLENECTOMY INFECTION
Loss of splenic immune function → severe sepsis risk from encapsulated organisms (S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, H. influenzae). Major long-term concern after splenectomy — especially pneumococcal infection.
Slide 48Splenectomy
  • Post Splenectomy Considerations:
    • Thrombocytosis
      • more common in myeloproliferative disorders (e.g CML)
      • Can cause life threatening thrombosis.
    • Overwhelming PostSplenctomy Infections ( OPSI)
      • Most common, fatal complication
      • Most commonly by S.pneumoniae
      • Greater among pt who had surgery for hematological or malignant conditions.
  • Septic shock a year after splenectomy → Streptococcus pneumoniae 438 ×2; fever and rash after splenectomy → OPSI. 441
Notes

Mastery Checklist — Splenic Disorders

1 Stable splenic trauma → try non-operative management; prefer selective over non-selective embolization when IR is
needed.
2 Pediatric patients: strong effort to preserve/delay splenectomy because of infectious risk.
3 Splenic artery aneurysm treatment triggers: pseudoaneurysm, symptomatic, or >2 cm; rupture risk is especially
dangerous in pregnancy.
4 Splenic pseudocysts are usually post-traumatic; true cysts are rare.
5 Non-Hodgkin lymphoma involves the spleen more than Hodgkin lymphoma; can cause hypersplenism.
6 ITP splenectomy indications: platelets <10,000/µL for ≥6 weeks, steroid-refractory, or steroid toxicity.

Indications for Splenectomy: A Comprehensive Guide

Splenectomy is performed for various medical conditions and surgical reasons, which can be broadly categorized into eight general indications:

1- Hypersplenism (Overactive Spleen)
  • Definition: An enlarged spleen (splenomegaly) that causes excessive destruction of blood cells (pancytopenia). Causes:
  • Hematologic disorders: Myeloproliferative diseases (CML, myelofibrosis), lymphoma.
  • Metabolic/storage diseases: Gaucher’s disease, Niemann-Pick disease.
  • Chronic infections: Malaria, tuberculosis.
  • Symptoms:
    • Pancytopenia (low RBCs, WBCs, platelets).
    • Early satiety (compression of the stomach).
  • Indications for Splenectomy:
  • Severe cytopenia refractory to medical treatment.
  • Symptomatic splenomegaly (pain, compression).
  • Risk of splenic rupture.
2- Autoimmune & Erythrocyte Disorders
  • Definition: Autoimmune-mediated destruction of blood cells or intrinsic RBC defects leading to splenic sequestration.
  • Examples:
  • Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) → Autoantibodies destroy platelets.
  • Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) → Antibodies destroy RBCs.
  • Hereditary spherocytosis → RBC membrane defect → early RBC destruction.
  • Indications for Splenectomy:
    • Severe, refractory cases unresponsive to steroids or immunosuppressants.
    • Frequent blood transfusion dependency.
    • Symptomatic anemia or thrombocytopenia.
3- Trauma & Splenic Injury
  • Definition: Damage to the spleen from blunt or penetrating trauma.
  • Common Causes:
  • Motor vehicle accidents (most common).
  • Sports injuries (football, skiing, etc.).
  • Ruptured splenic artery aneurysm.
  • Indications for Splenectomy:
    • Hemodynamic instability despite resuscitation.
    • Grade IV–V splenic injury (per AAST classification).
    • Splenic rupture with active bleeding.
    • Massive hemoperitoneum.
    • Alternative: Splenic preservation (angiographic embolization) is preferred when feasible.
4- Vascular diseases of the Spleen
  • Definition: Conditions affecting splenic circulation that may require splenectomy.
  • Examples:
  • Splenic vein thrombosis → Can cause left-sided portal hypertension & variceal bleeding.
  • Splenic artery aneurysm → Risk of rupture & life-threatening hemorrhage.
  • Indications for Splenectomy:
    • Symptomatic splenic vein thrombosis with variceal bleeding.
    • Large (>2 cm) or ruptured splenic artery aneurysms.
5- Cysts, Abscesses, & Primary Splenic Tumors
  • Definition: Mass lesions affecting the spleen.
  • Examples:
  • Splenic cysts (e.g., simple cysts, echinococcal cysts).
  • Splenic abscess (bacterial, fungal, or parasitic).
  • Benign tumors (hemangioma, lymphangioma, hamartoma).
  • Malignant tumors (primary splenic lymphoma, metastatic tumors).
  • Indications for Splenectomy:
    • Large symptomatic cysts (>5 cm).
    • Persistent or multiple abscesses despite antibiotic therapy.
    • Neoplasms causing pain, hypersplenism, or suspicion of malignancy.
    • Alternatives:
    • Percutaneous drainage (for some cysts & abscesses).
    • Partial splenectomy (for select cases).
6- Diagnostic Splenectomy
  • Definition: Removal of the spleen to establish a definitive diagnosis when other methods fail.
  • Examples:
  • Suspected lymphoma or leukemia when bone marrow biopsy is inconclusive.
  • Atypical presentations of hematologic disorders.
  • Indications for Splenectomy:
    • When a diagnostic biopsy is not possible (e.g., deep-seated lymphoma).
    • Unexplained splenomegaly with uncertain cause.
    • Alternative: Core needle biopsy or fine-needle aspiration when feasible.
7- Iatrogenic Splenectomy (Accidental Injury During Surgery)
  • Definition: Unintentional splenic removal due to intraoperative trauma.
  • Causes:
  • Difficult abdominal surgeries (e.g., distal pancreatectomy, gastric resection).
  • Uncontrolled intraoperative bleeding from splenic vessels.
  • Indications for Splenectomy:
    • Irreparable splenic laceration during surgery.
    • Massive bleeding during intra-abdominal procedures.
8- Incidental Splenectomy (Planned Spleen Removal During Other Surgery)
  • Definition: Planned splenectomy as part of another operation.
  • Examples:
  • Distal pancreatectomy (due to shared vascular supply).
  • Resection of left-sided renal/adrenal tumors.
  • Gastric cancer or retroperitoneal sarcoma with direct invasion.
  • Indications for Splenectomy:
    • Tumor invasion of the splenic hilum.
    • Involvement of splenic vessels requiring resection.

Clinical Presentation
Symptoms depend on the underlying cause but commonly include:
  • Fatigue (due to anemia).
  • Easy bruising & bleeding (due to thrombocytopenia).
  • Frequent infections (due to leukopenia).
  • Abdominal discomfort or fullness (especially in large spleens).
  • Early satiety (spleen compressing stomach).
  • Hematemesis (vomiting blood from esophageal varices in portal hypertension).
Physical Exam:
  • Splenomegaly (enlarged spleen) is often palpable.
  • Signs of anemia (pallor, tachycardia).
  • Petechiae or purpura (suggestive of thrombocytopenia).
Diagnostic Workup
Laboratory Findings:
  • Pancytopenia (low RBCs, WBCs, and platelets).
  • Elevated reticulocyte count (compensatory bone marrow response).
  • Increased indirect bilirubin & LDH (suggestive of hemolysis).
  • Bone marrow biopsy (to rule out primary marrow failure).
Imaging:
  • Ultrasound/CT scan:
  • Confirms splenomegaly.
  • Differentiates spleen from other abdominal masses.
  • MRI: Preferred for storage diseases (e.g., Gaucher’s).
  • Bone Marrow Aspiration & Biopsy:
  • Needed for leukemia, lymphoma, or aplastic anemia diagnosis.

Management & Treatment Options
1️- Medical Treatment (Preferred First-Line)
Treatment is directed at the underlying cause:
  • Cirrhosis & Portal Hypertension → Treat liver disease, TIPS procedure for variceal bleeding.
  • Autoimmune Disorders (ITP, AIHA) → Steroids, IVIG, rituximab before considering surgery.
  • Myeloproliferative Disorders (CML, Myelofibrosis) → Cytoreductive therapy (hydroxyurea, JAK inhibitors).
  • Infections (Malaria, TB, Leishmaniasis) → Antimicrobial therapy.
2️- Splenectomy (For Refractory or Severe Cases)
Approach:
  • Laparoscopic splenectomy (preferred for smaller spleens).
  • Open splenectomy (for massive splenomegaly > 1500 g).
Preoperative Considerations:
  • Vaccination against encapsulated bacteria (H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis).
  • Platelet transfusions if thrombocytopenia is severe.
3️- Alternatives to Splenectomy
  • Splenic artery embolization (for selected cases to reduce spleen size).
  • Radiotherapy (used in rare cases of hypersplenism due to lymphoma).
Prognosis & Outcomes
Depends on the underlying cause:
  • Excellent prognosis in hereditary spherocytosis, ITP, & thalassemia after splenectomy.
  • Poorer prognosis in myelofibrosis, leukemia, cirrhosis with portal hypertension.
  • Splenectomy improves:
  • Hemoglobin levels & reduces transfusion needs.
  • Platelet counts (reducing bleeding risks).
  • Risk of Overwhelming Post-Splenectomy Infection (OPSI):
  • Mortality rate up to 50% if sepsis develops.
  • Lifelong vaccinations & prophylactic antibiotics may be needed.
Neoplastic Diseases & The Role of Splenectomy
1️- Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL)
  • Definition: A low-grade B-cell leukemia, most common in the elderly.
  • Key Features:
  • Accumulation of functionally incompetent B lymphocytes.
  • Indolent course, but later stages involve splenomegaly & cytopenias (due to hypersplenism & marrow infiltration).
  • Complications: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA), thrombocytopenia, and infection risk.
  • Indications for Splenectomy in CLL:
  • Refractory cytopenias (anemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia) despite treatment.
  • Massive splenomegaly causing pain or mechanical symptoms.
  • Hypersplenism leading to transfusion dependency.
  • Patients not responding to targeted therapies (e.g., rituximab, ibrutinib).
Contraindications:
  • Severe bone marrow failure (splenectomy will not help if marrow is the primary problem).
  • Poor performance status (high surgical risk in frail patients).
Response to Splenectomy:
  • Platelets improve in 70-85% of cases.
  • Neutrophils improve in 60-70% of cases.
  • Anemia improves in ~50% of cases.
  • Median duration of benefit: >1 year.
2️- Hairy Cell Leukemia (HCL)
  • Definition: A rare B-cell malignancy, comprising ~2% of leukemias.
  • Key Features:
  • Pancytopenia (anemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia).
  • Splenomegaly (80% of cases, often massive).
  • "Hairy cells" on peripheral smear (lymphocytes with cytoplasmic projections).
  • Current first-line therapy: Purine nucleoside analogs (cladribine, pentostatin) → 80-90% complete remission.
  • Splenectomy was the standard before 1995 but is now only used for palliation in:
  • Massive, symptomatic splenomegaly.
  • Persistent cytopenias despite chemotherapy.

No proven survival benefit of splenectomy in HCL.

3️- Myelodysplastic Syndrome (MDS) & Myelofibrosis
  • Definition: A stem cell disorder leading to ineffective hematopoiesis and bone marrow failure.
  • Key Features:
  • Pancytopenia (anemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia).
  • Extramedullary hematopoiesis (liver, spleen).
  • Progression to acute myeloid leukemia (AML) in some cases.
  • Indications for Splenectomy in Myelofibrosis:
  • Severe splenomegaly with mass effect (pain, early satiety).
  • Refractory cytopenias (hemolysis, thrombocytopenia).
  • Portal hypertension with variceal bleeding.
Surgical Risks:
  • High operative mortality (7-10%).
  • Frequent postoperative complications (hepatic dysfunction, infections).
Outcome of Splenectomy:
  • Improves anemia & thrombocytopenia in ~75% of patients.
  • Relieves symptoms of splenomegaly.
  • Does not improve overall survival significantly.
4️- Systemic Mast Cell Disease (Mastocytosis)
  • Definition: A rare condition with mast cell infiltration of multiple organs, including the spleen.
  • Types:
  • Indolent → Benign, no need for splenectomy.
  • Aggressive → Associated with hematologic malignancies.
  • Indications for Splenectomy in Mastocytosis:
  • Severe thrombocytopenia due to hypersplenism.
  • Massive splenomegaly with symptoms.
  • Improves survival in aggressive mastocytosis with cytopenias.
Alternative Therapies:
  • Interferon-alpha.
  • Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) (e.g., imatinib in selected cases).

Metabolic Disorders & Splenectomy
1️- Gaucher Disease
  • Definition: Autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder due to β- glucosidase deficiency.
  • Pathophysiology:
  • Accumulation of glucocerebroside in macrophages (Gaucher cells).
  • Infiltration of spleen, liver, bone marrow → hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, bone disease.
  • Types:
  • Type I (non-neuropathic) → Most common, amenable to splenectomy.
  • Type II & III → Neuropathic forms, splenectomy not indicated.
  • First-line therapy: Enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) (imiglucerase, velaglucerase, taliglucerase).
  • Indications for Splenectomy:
    • Severe, refractory thrombocytopenia (risk of bleeding).
    • Massive splenomegaly causing pain, early satiety, or mechanical complications.
    • Bone marrow failure due to hypersplenism.
Partial vs. Total Splenectomy:
  • Total splenectomy is preferred if medically necessary.
  • Partial splenectomy is rarely performed due to high recurrence rates & complications.
Prognosis:
  • ERT is highly effective, reducing need for splenectomy.
  • Splenectomy does not cure Gaucher disease but improves symptoms in severe cases.
2️- Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome (WAS)
  • Definition: X-linked disorder causing:
  • Thrombocytopenia (small platelets, easy bleeding).
  • Combined B- & T-cell immunodeficiency.
  • Eczema & high risk of malignancies (lymphoma, leukemia).
  • Symptoms:
  • Petechiae, purpura, recurrent infections, bloody diarrhea.
  • Increased risk of autoimmune disorders & malignancies.
  • First-line treatment:
  • Prophylactic antibiotics & IV immunoglobulin (IVIG).
  • Bone marrow transplantation (BMT) → Curative if matched donor available.
  • Indications for Splenectomy:
  • Severe thrombocytopenia (platelets <20,000/μL) with bleeding.
  • Failure of medical therapy.
Risks of Splenectomy:
  • Increased infection risk (especially encapsulated bacteria).
  • Requires lifelong antibiotic prophylaxis (penicillin) & vaccinations (pneumococcus, meningococcus, Hib).
Prognosis:
  • Without BMT → poor survival due to infections & malignancies.
  • With splenectomy → improved platelet counts but does not correct immune deficiency.
3️- Chediak-Higashi Syndrome
  • Definition: Rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by:
  • Defective lysosomal trafficking → giant granules in leukocytes.
  • Immunodeficiency → recurrent bacterial infections.
  • Neurological symptoms → nystagmus, ataxia.
  • Accelerated phase (hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, HLH).
  • First-line therapy:
  • Bone marrow transplantation (BMT) → only curative option.
  • Steroids, chemotherapy, ascorbic acid (vitamin C).
  • Indications for Splenectomy:
  • Accelerated phase with severe splenomegaly & cytopenias.
  • Severe hemophagocytic syndrome.
Prognosis:
  • Poor without BMT.
  • Splenectomy may provide symptomatic relief but is not curative.
4️- Sarcoidosis
  • Definition: Multisystem granulomatous disease of unknown etiology.
  • Pathophysiology:
  • Non-caseating granulomas in multiple organs.
  • Lungs most commonly affected, but spleen involved in ~50-60% of cases. ✔ Symptoms of Splenic Sarcoidosis:
  • Splenomegaly (rarely massive).
  • Cytopenias (pancytopenia due to hypersplenism).
  • Hypercalcemia & constitutional symptoms.
  • First-line therapy: Corticosteroids, methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine.
  • Indications for Splenectomy:
  • Severe, symptomatic splenomegaly.
  • Refractory cytopenias despite medical treatment.
  • Hypercalcemia not controlled by steroids.
Prognosis:
  • Most patients respond to steroids.
  • Splenectomy provides symptom relief but does not treat underlying disease.

Erythrocyte Disorders & Splenectomy
1️- Hereditary Spherocytosis (HS)
  • Definition: Most common inherited hemolytic anemia (1 in 5000) caused by mutations in RBC cytoskeletal proteins (ankyrin, spectrin, band 3, protein 4.2).
  • Pathophysiology:
  • Defective RBC membrane → Spherical RBCs (spherocytes).
  • Decreased deformability → Splenic sequestration & destruction.

Clinical Features: Triad: Anemia, jaundice, splenomegaly.

  • Gallstones (pigment stones in ~85% of adults).
  • Hemolytic crises (exacerbations after infections).
  • Aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19 infection).
Diagnosis:
  • Peripheral smear → Spherocytes (small, round RBCs lacking central pallor).
  • Osmotic fragility test → Increased RBC hemolysis in hypotonic solution.
  • Negative Coombs test → Rules out autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
  • ↑ Reticulocyte count, LDH, bilirubin; ↓ Haptoglobin (signs of hemolysis).
  • First-line: Folic acid supplementation, blood transfusions.
  • Splenectomy if:
  • Severe anemia requiring transfusions.
  • Symptomatic splenomegaly.
  • Complications (e.g., gallstones, leg ulcers, aplastic crises).
  • Children ≥6 years (delayed to avoid post-splenectomy infections).
  • Partial splenectomy in children <5 years with severe disease.
Prognosis:
  • Splenectomy normalizes RBC lifespan → Cures anemia & jaundice.
  • Spherocytes persist, but hemolysis stops.
  • Risk of post-splenectomy infections → Lifelong vaccinations & prophylaxis needed.
2️- Hereditary Elliptocytosis (Ovalocytosis)
  • Definition: Autosomal dominant defect in spectrin → Oval-shaped RBCs.
  • Mild or asymptomatic in most cases (~90%).
  • Symptoms: Mild anemia, jaundice, splenomegaly.
  • Diagnosis:
  • Peripheral smear → >2️5️% elliptical RBCs.
  • Osmotic fragility test → Increased hemolysis (less than HS).
  • When is Splenectomy Indicated?
  • For symptomatic patients only (anemia, gallstones).
  • Cholecystectomy if gallstones present.
  • Splenectomy improves anemia but does not change RBC shape.
3️- Hereditary Nonspherocytic Hemolytic Anemia
  • Definition: Group of inherited hemolytic anemias caused by enzyme defects (e.g., pyruvate kinase deficiency, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency).
  • Pathophysiology:
  • Defective RBC metabolism → Oxidative stress & hemolysis.
  • Splenic sequestration worsens hemolysis.
  • Clinical Features:
  • Jaundice, anemia, gallstones, splenomegaly.
  • Triggered by infections, medications, or foods (e.g., fava beans in G6PD deficiency).
  • Diagnosis:
  • Peripheral smear → Bite cells, Heinz bodies (denatured hemoglobin).
  • Enzyme assays → ↓ Pyruvate kinase, ↓ G6️PD levels.
  • When is Splenectomy Indicated?
  • Splenectomy in Pyruvate Kinase Deficiency:
    • Reduces hemolysis & transfusion requirements.
  • Not useful in G6PD Deficiency:
    • Avoid oxidative triggers instead.
4️- Thalassemia Major (Cooley’s Anemia)
  • Definition: Autosomal recessive disorder affecting hemoglobin synthesis.
  • Pathophysiology:
  • Defective β-globin (β-thalassemia major) → Excess α-globin → RBC destruction.
  • Severe anemia, ineffective erythropoiesis, and hemolysis.
  • Clinical Features:
  • Severe anemia from infancy → Requires lifelong transfusions.
  • Hepatosplenomegaly (due to extramedullary hematopoiesis).
  • Skeletal deformities (frontal bossing, chipmunk facies).
  • Iron overload (from transfusions → Risk of organ failure).
  • Diagnosis:
  • Peripheral smear → Target cells, nucleated RBCs, microcytic hypochromic anemia.
  • Hemoglobin electrophoresis → ↑ HbF, ↓ HbA, ↑ HbA2.
  • When is Splenectomy Indicated?
  • Not curative, but considered in severe cases:
    • Massive splenomegaly causing symptoms.
    • High transfusion requirements.
    • Hypersplenism worsening anemia & thrombocytopenia.
  • Prognosis:
  • Splenectomy reduces transfusion needs but does not cure the disease.
  • Iron overload still needs management (iron chelation therapy).
  • Bone marrow transplant is the only curative option.

Autoimmune Disorders & Splenectomy
1️- Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia (AIHA)
  • Definition: IgG autoantibodies against RBC membranes lead to premature RBC destruction.
  • Pathophysiology:
  • Warm AIHA (IgG-mediated) → Splenic macrophages destroy RBCs.
  • Cold AIHA (IgM-mediated) → Intravascular hemolysis (NOT spleen- dependent).
  • Clinical Features:
  • Anemia, jaundice, splenomegaly.
  • Pigment gallstones (due to chronic hemolysis).
  • Severe cases → Hemoglobinuria, renal failure.
  • Diagnosis:
  • Positive Direct Coombs test (IgG or complement-coated RBCs).
  • Peripheral smear → Spherocytes, polychromasia.
  • ↑ Reticulocytes, LDH, bilirubin; ↓ Haptoglobin.
  • First-line: Corticosteroids (75% response).
  • Splenectomy if:
  • Steroid-resistant or steroid-dependent disease.
  • Relapses after steroid withdrawal.
  • Severe hemolysis requiring frequent transfusions.
  • NOT effective for Cold AIHA (complement-mediated, not spleen- dependent).
  • Prognosis:
  • 50-60% response rate after splenectomy.
  • If unresponsive, second-line therapy = Rituximab, immunosuppressants.
2️- Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP)
  • Definition: Autoimmune platelet destruction due to IgG antibodies against glycoprotein IIb/IIIa.
  • Pathophysiology:
  • Spleen removes antibody-coated platelets → Thrombocytopenia.
  • Spleen may also be a site of antibody production.
  • Clinical Features:
  • Petechiae, purpura, easy bruising, epistaxis, gum bleeding.
  • NO splenomegaly (except in secondary causes).
  • Diagnosis:
  • ↓ Platelet count (<100,000/μL).
  • ↑ Megakaryocytes in bone marrow (compensatory response).
  • Normal PT, PTT, and fibrinogen (to rule out DIC).
  • Positive platelet-associated antibodies (confirmatory but not required).
  • First-line: Corticosteroids (60-80% response).
  • Second-line: Rituximab, IVIG, thrombopoietin receptor agonists.
  • Splenectomy if:
  • Failure to respond to steroids.
  • Relapse after initial response.
  • Steroid dependence.
  • Severe thrombocytopenia with bleeding risk.
  • Not first-line for HIV-associated ITP (high infection risk post- splenectomy).
  • Prognosis:
  • Splenectomy is curative in ~80% of cases.
  • Post-splenectomy thrombocytosis may occur.
  • Vaccination against encapsulated bacteria required before surgery.
3️- Felty Syndrome (RA + Splenomegaly + Neutropenia)
  • Definition: A rare complication of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) with splenomegaly & neutropenia.
  • Pathophysiology:
  • IgG-coated neutrophils are destroyed in the spleen → Recurrent infections.
  • T-cell dysregulation contributes to neutropenia.
  • Clinical Features:
  • Severe RA symptoms (joint pain, swelling, deformities).
  • Recurrent bacterial infections (due to neutropenia).
  • Splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy.
  • Diagnosis:
  • ↓ Neutrophil count (<1,500/μL).
  • ↑ Rheumatoid factor (RF), anti-CCP antibodies.
  • Bone marrow biopsy → Normal or hyperplastic myeloid cells.
  • First-line: Methotrexate, corticosteroids, G-CSF (granulocyte colony- stimulating factor).
  • Splenectomy if:
  • Severe neutropenia unresponsive to medical therapy.
  • Recurrent, life-threatening infections.
  • Prognosis:
  • Neutropenia improves in 60-70% after splenectomy.
  • Risk of recurrence despite normal neutrophil count.
  • Not a definitive cure, as RA progression continues.
4️- Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP)
  • Definition: A life-threatening disorder characterized by widespread platelet aggregation & microvascular thrombosis.
  • Pathophysiology:
  • Deficiency of ADAMTS13 enzyme → Uncontrolled vWF multimers → Platelet clumping → Thrombocytopenia, hemolysis, ischemia.
  • Clinical Features: Pentad of TTP: 1. Thrombocytopenia (petechiae, purpura). 2. Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes on smear). 3. Neurologic symptoms (confusion, seizures, stroke). 4. Renal failure. 5. Fever.
  • Diagnosis:
  • Peripheral smear → Schistocytes, helmet cells.
  • ↓ Platelets, ↓ Haptoglobin, ↑ LDH, ↑ Indirect bilirubin (signs of hemolysis).
  • Normal PT & PTT (to differentiate from DIC).
  • ↓ ADAMTS13 activity, ↑ vWF multimers (confirmatory).
  • First-line: Plasmapheresis + corticosteroids + rituximab (complete response in 55-65%).
  • Splenectomy if:
  • Refractory to plasma exchange & steroids.
  • Frequent relapses.
  • Prognosis:
  • Plasmapheresis improves survival (~90%).
  • Splenectomy helps in refractory cases but has a 20-30% relapse rate.

Vascular Disorders, Cysts, Tumors, and Infections of the Spleen
1️- Splenic Vein Thrombosis (SVT)
  • Definition: Thrombosis (clot formation) in the splenic vein, leading to gastric varices and upper gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding.
  • Most Common Cause: Pancreatitis (acute/chronic) or pancreatic pseudocyst (20% of cases).
  • Other Causes:
  • Pancreatic or gastric malignancies.
  • Posterior gastric ulcer (local inflammation).
  • Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis.
  • Clinical Features:
  • Upper GI bleeding due to isolated gastric varices (fundal location).
  • Splenomegaly without generalized portal hypertension.
  • No esophageal varices (differentiates from portal hypertension).
  • Diagnosis:
  • Contrast-enhanced CT/MRI → Shows absence of blood flow in the splenic vein.
  • High-resolution ultrasound → May be used but can be limited by bowel gas.
  • Endoscopy → Reveals isolated gastric varices.
  • When is Splenectomy Indicated?
  • Splenectomy is curative (removes venous congestion → stops variceal bleeding).
  • Prophylactic splenectomy for patients with SVT + gastric varices, even without prior bleeding.
  • Portal vein thrombosis → Splenectomy is NOT effective.
  • Prognosis:
  • Excellent outcome with splenectomy (eliminates gastric varices).
  • If untreated, risk of life-threatening GI bleeding remains.
2️- Cysts & Tumors of the Spleen
  • Definition: Benign and malignant lesions of the spleen.
  • Types:
  • Parasitic cysts (Echinococcus → hydatid cyst).
  • Non-parasitic cysts (dermoid, epidermoid, endothelial, pseudocysts).
  • Benign tumors (hemangioma, hamartoma).
  • Malignant tumors (sarcoma, lymphoma, metastatic tumors).
A. Parasitic Cysts (Echinococcus)
  • Hydatid cysts due to Echinococcus infection.
  • X-ray → May show calcified cyst wall.
  • Diagnosis:
  • Serologic tests (Echinococcus antibodies).
  • CT/MRI → Defines cyst characteristics.
  • Treatment:
  • Splenectomy is the treatment of choice.
  • Avoid cyst rupture (risk of anaphylaxis).
B. Non-Parasitic Cysts
  • Epidermoid, dermoid, endothelial cysts → Usually congenital.
  • Pseudocysts → Result from trauma or infarction.
  • Management:
  • Small, asymptomatic cysts → Observation.
  • Symptomatic or large cysts (>5 cm) → Partial splenectomy or total splenectomy.
C. Benign Tumors
  • Hemangioma, hamartoma:
  • Often asymptomatic.
  • May cause hypersplenism (pancytopenia).
  • Splenectomy if symptomatic or large (risk of rupture).
D. Malignant Tumors
  • Primary Splenic Malignancies: Rare but include sarcoma, lymphoma.
  • Metastases:
  • Commonly from lung cancer, breast cancer, melanoma.
  • Often found on autopsy and clinically silent.
  • Treatment:
  • Splenectomy if tumor is localized.
  • For widespread metastases, systemic therapy is preferred.
3️- Infections of the Spleen (Splenic Abscess)
  • Definition: Localized infection of the spleen, often secondary to hematogenous spread of bacteria.
  • Causes:
  • Infective endocarditis (most common).
  • IV drug use (septic emboli).
  • Infected splenic hematoma (trauma-related).
  • Direct spread from adjacent organs (pancreatitis, gastric perforation).
  • Clinical Features:
  • Fever, left upper quadrant (LUQ) pain, splenomegaly.
  • Left pleural effusion (suggests splenic involvement).
  • Persistent sepsis despite antibiotic therapy.
  • Diagnosis:
  • CT scan → Gold standard, shows hypodense lesion with rim enhancement.
  • Blood cultures → Identifies causative organism.
  • Leukocytosis → Suggests ongoing infection.
  • Splenectomy is the definitive treatment.
  • Percutaneous drainage:
  • Only for patients unfit for surgery.
  • High failure rate & recurrence risk.
  • Prognosis:
  • Mortality rate is 40-100% without treatment.
  • Early splenectomy reduces risk of rupture & sepsis.

Diagnostic, Iatrogenic, and Incidental Splenectomy
1️- Diagnostic Splenectomy
  • Definition: Removal of the spleen when other diagnostic methods fail to identify the cause of a disease.
  • Indications:
  • Unexplained splenic mass → 60% are malignant (mostly lymphomas; others may be metastatic carcinomas).
  • Splenomegaly of unknown cause → May be lymphoproliferative, granulomatous, or benign vascular lesions.
  • Failure of imaging and biopsy to establish a diagnosis.

  • MRI with gadolinium contrast is best for diagnosing benign hemangiomas.
2️- Splenectomy for Staging of Hodgkin’s Lymphoma (Historical)
  • Definition: Previously used to assess the extent of Hodgkin lymphoma and guide treatment.
  • Systemic chemotherapy treats the whole body → No need for invasive staging.
  • PET/CT scanning provides accurate staging without surgery.
  • Current Role: Rarely performed except in highly selected cases.
3️- Iatrogenic Splenectomy (Accidental Removal)
  • Definition: Splenectomy performed unintentionally due to injury during surgery.
  • Common Causes:
  • Mobilization of the spleen during left upper quadrant surgery:
    • Left adrenalectomy.
    • Left nephrectomy.
    • Splenic flexure mobilization during colectomy.
  • Bleeding from small splenic capsular vessels during manipulation.
  • Anti-reflux surgery complications:
    • A national study showed a 2.3% risk of iatrogenic splenectomy during Nissen fundoplication (anti-reflux surgery).
  • Splenic trauma from colonoscopy:
    • Rare but reported cases of splenic rupture due to excessive force.
4️- Incidental Splenectomy (Planned Removal During Other Surgery)
  • Definition: Intentional removal of the spleen during another major surgery.
  • Most Common Indications:
  • Distal pancreatectomy for pancreatic tumors.
  • Proximal gastric cancer resection (for lymph node clearance).
  • Large retroperitoneal tumors (sarcomas, renal cell carcinoma, adrenal tumors) that invade the spleen.
  • Lymph node dissection in gastric and esophageal cancer.
  • Can the Spleen Be Preserved?
  • Yes, in selected cases.
  • Techniques for spleen-preserving distal pancreatectomy:
  • Preserving splenic artery & vein.
  • Ligation of splenic artery but keeping short gastric vessels intact.
  • Laparoscopic and robotic approaches can enhance splenic preservation.
  • When Must the Spleen Be Removed?
  • Tumors involving the splenic hilum.
  • Lymphoma requiring nodal clearance.
  • Malignant invasion of the spleen.
5️- Splenosis (Autotransplantation of Splenic Tissue)
  • Definition: The accidental transplantation of splenic fragments throughout the abdomen following splenic rupture or surgery.
  • Key Features:
  • Splenic tissue implants & grows on peritoneal surfaces.
  • Mimics peritoneal metastases on imaging.
  • May cause adhesions & bowel obstruction.
  • Diagnosis:
  • 99mTc-labeled heat-damaged red blood cell scan → Confirms functioning splenic tissue.
  • Management:
  • No intervention unless symptomatic.
  • Must be distinguished from peritoneal cancer or lymphoma.

Splenectomy: Preoperative, Surgical Techniques, and Postoperative
Considerations
1️- Preoperative Preparation
Optimize Hematologic Parameters:
  • Correct anemia and coagulation abnormalities.
  • Treat infections preoperatively.
  • Control immune reactions in autoimmune disorders.
Vaccination (Crucial for Prevention of Post-Splenectomy Sepsis):
  • Pneumococcal vaccine (PCV13 & PPSV23) – prevents infections by encapsulated organisms.
  • Haemophilus influenzae type B (Hib) vaccine.
  • Meningococcal vaccine (MenACWY).
  • Influenza vaccine (annually).
Blood Transfusion Considerations:
  • Cross-matching may be complicated by autoantibodies.
  • Platelet transfusion should be given only after splenic artery ligation (prevents rapid sequestration).
Steroid Coverage for Autoimmune Conditions:
  • Patients on chronic corticosteroids should receive stress-dose steroids perioperatively.
Emergency Splenectomy Preparation:
  • Correct hypovolemia using whole blood or packed RBC transfusions.
2️- Surgical Techniques
A. Open Splenectomy
Two Main Approaches:

1. Traditional Approach (Used in trauma cases) 2. Massive Splenomegaly Approach (For extremely large spleens)

B. Laparoscopic Splenectomy (Preferred for Elective Cases)

Standard of Care in most high-volume centers.

Suitable for:
  • Idiopathic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP).
  • Hereditary Spherocytosis.
  • Small to moderate-sized spleens.
Contraindications:
  • Massive splenomegaly.
  • Portal hypertension (risk of excessive bleeding).
  • Severe cardiopulmonary comorbidities.
Advantages:
  • Less postoperative pain.
  • Shorter hospital stay.
  • Faster recovery.
Laparoscopic Partial Splenectomy:
  • Used for benign focal lesions or hereditary hematologic disorders.
  • Preserves splenic immune function.
3️- Splenorrhaphy (Splenic Repair)

Used when splenic preservation is feasible after trauma.

Partial Splenectomy:
Indications:
  • Gaucher disease (to reduce cytopenia).
  • Large cysts or benign tumors.
  • Higher complication rates than complete splenectomy.
  • Not suitable for autoimmune diseases → Total splenectomy is required to prevent recurrence.
4️- Hematologic Effects of Splenectomy
Red Blood Cell Changes:
  • Howell-Jolly bodies (nuclear remnants).
  • Heinz bodies (denatured hemoglobin).
  • Target cells & siderocytes.
Leukocytosis:
  • Initial granulocytosis → Later replaced by lymphocytosis & monocytosis.
Thrombocytosis:
  • Transient in most patients.
  • Persistent in 10-20% of cases.
  • Extreme thrombocytosis (>1 million/µL) can increase clot risk.
  • Management:
  • Aspirin or clopidogrel may help prevent thrombosis.
  • Anticoagulation NOT routinely needed.

2️- Long-Term Risks & Overwhelming Post-Splenectomy Infection (OPSI)
OPSI: A Life-Threatening Emergency
  • OPSI is a rapid, fulminant bacteremia that can be fatal within 24-48 hours.
  • Risk is highest in:
  • Children under 2 years.
  • Within the first 2 years post-splenectomy (80% of cases).
  • Patients with hematologic disorders (e.g., hemolytic anemias, lymphoma).
  • Pathophysiology:
  • Reduced clearance of bacteria from blood.
  • Lower levels of IgM.
  • Decreased opsonization activity → leads to severe sepsis and shock.
  • Most Common Pathogens:
  • Streptococcus pneumoniae (most frequent cause).
  • Haemophilus influenzae.
  • Neisseria meningitidis.
  • Clinical Presentation:
  • Initial flu-like symptoms (malaise, fever, myalgia).
  • Rapid progression to septic shock (high fever, hypotension, DIC).
  • Mortality rate ~50% if not treated promptly.

Persistent Thrombocytosis
  • Platelet counts may exceed 1,000,000/µL.
  • Increased risk of DVT, PE, and portal vein thrombosis.
  • Management:
  • Aspirin (81-325 mg daily) for antiplatelet therapy.
  • Anticoagulation (DOAC/warfarin) if thrombosis develops.
Increased Risk of Thrombosis
  • Portal vein thrombosis (PVT) (3% incidence).
  • Venous thromboembolism (VTE, DVT, PE) risk increased.
  • Management:
  • Prophylactic anticoagulation in high-risk patients.
  • Monitor liver function tests (signs of portal hypertension).
